AI will intuitively become super useful in many areas beyond math, without that implying universal advances.

There's probably a lot of low hanging fruit out there where the current total knowledge of humanity more than suffices to solve a problem but experts aren't connecting. Say, a local species that is unknown to biologists but present in local records, or a historical mystery that is explained by material science.

Consider, however, that to improve a drug you need to observe 10-year survival rates. The machine can hardly wait those ten years any quicker than we do. They can't operate in physical space yet either, so if your historical problem requires excavating a site rather than exploring digitized records AI is toast there as well. Experimental sciences seem to be the last to survive, then.

I'm starting to see the pattern that pure intellectual work will be gradually commoditized, and physical labor is where value will exist. Which is quite a flip, a scary one.

(This is also interesting as a(nother) example of the difficulty of making truly correct software -- you'd hope for proof-checker kernels to be pretty high on the correctness scale but seems like we've found 16-32 soundness bugs in a bunch of these.)

It's been a year and a half since this paper, so they've likely done a lot more research in this area and, specifically, on eliciting this sort of behavior in post-training. The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. There's some AI traders to keep the market moving, but they drop out in any round that has more than five people. They operate using a naive set of rules that I wrote for them, so they're not too hard to beat -- it's when the market is full of real people that it gets tricky.
